senses: collected into a ball, heap, or mass
ety: From Latin agglomerātus, past participle of agglomerō (“to wind into a ball”), from ad- (“to”) + glomerō (“to wind into a ball”), from glomus (“a ball”), akin to globus (“a ball”).

senses: The state or condition of being bistable.
A flamenco dance associated with Andalusia.
A non-SI unit of energy equal to 1,000 calories (small calories), used (now rare) in chemistry or physics; equal to 1 calorie as used in nutrition. Symbol kcal.
Visually suggestive of a swirl, whorl, or vortex.
That moves in a whirling motion.
examples: The whirly pattern on the wallpaper.
The whirly blades on top of a helicopter.
He was studying this brolga dance which was being performed with the accompaniment of a whirly haze of dust sprayed from the rusty wrecks of car bodies strewn over the flats behind them.

senses: The wrinkling of the brows or face in frowning; the expression of displeasure, sullenness, or discontent in the countenance; an angry frown.
Gloom; dark or threatening aspect.
ety: From Middle English scowlen, scoulen, skoulen (also as Middle English schoulen), probably of North Germanic origin. Compare Danish skule (“to scowl”), Norwegian skule (“to scowl”).

senses: An electromagnetic wave refracted back to the Earth by the ionosphere.
A type of sushi with rice wrapped in a pouch of fried tofu (aburaage).
Having a specified type of radius.
Having a rounded or curved edge.
ety: From radius + -ed. Piecewise doublet of rayed.

senses: A Chinese gooseberry vine fruit, having a hairy brown skin and dark green (or in the case of the gold kiwifruit, yellow) flesh with fine black seeds, almost always Actinidia chinensis var. deliciosa.
ety: From Kiwi /kiwi (“of or from New Zealand”) + fruit; a trade name used by exporters for one of several varieties selectively bred in New Zealand.
examples: The international threat isn't coming from New Zealand, whose growing season does not conflict with California's. New Zealand kiwifruit is marketed in the summer months; California's season is from November through May.

Vitamin C values increased from 65.92 ± 9.1 (day 0) to 102 ± 23.1 μM (day 28) and from 68 ± 15.2 μM to 92.38 ± 14.7 μM after consuming two and three kiwifruit per day, respectively (Duttaroy & Jorgensen, 2004).
In the produce industry, a long shelf life is critical to success, too. (One hard lesson: Pre-peeled kiwifruit is not a good idea.)

senses: A genre of Cape Verdean music and dance.
A piece of music in this style.
To form a pus-filled cavity, typically from an infection.
ety: Borrowed from Latin abscessus (“a going away; gathering of humors, abscess”), from abscēdō (“go away, depart”), from abs (“away from”) + cēdō (“go”). See cede.

senses: A form of mallet used to beat meat before cooking.
A tool similar to a potato masher used for tenderizing
A tool with nails or blades, that can be pressed on (not unlike a stapler) to puncture the meat.
A person who windsurfs.
A singer, particularly a professional singer who performs ballads.
A Roman helmet.
Having uncontrolled excitement; ecstatic.
ety: From delirium + -ous; see also Latin delirus (“silly, doting, crazy”).

senses: Someone who tries to conform to the mainstream.
A noctuid moth (Lithophane furcifera)
The inclusions and fissures within an emerald.
ety: From French jardin (“garden”), from the mossy appearance. Doublet of garden.

senses: A vivid red dye made from the dried bodies of cochineal insects.
The vivid red colour of this dye.
ety: The noun is borrowed from Middle French cochenille (modern French cochenille), from Italian cocciniglia or Spanish cochinilla; further etymology uncertain, possibly from Latin coccineus, coccinus (“scarlet-dyed; scarlet in colour”) (whence Italian coccineo (“scarlet in colour”)) + Italian -iglia (suffix forming collective nouns), Spanish -illa (“diminutive suffix”). A device that generates a code, often as a series of pulses.
A person who assigns codes or classifications.
the room reserved for males and their activities, often in the lower part of the house.
ety: Latin andron, from Ancient Greek ἀνδρών (andrṓn).

senses: To coat (steel, etc.) with an oxalate.
ety: Probably directly from the noun, through the influence of -ate (verb-forming suffix).

senses: Incidentally; in passing.
examples: I will not here stand to discuss obiter, whether stars be causes, or signs; or to apologize for judicial astrology.

senses: A polyphenol, or derivative
The process by which multiple recorded sounds are combined into one or more channels.
An expert at microscopy.
A vocal exercise performed by singing one or more vowels without actually forming any words.
One who or that which helps something to happen.
One who encourages a bad habit in another (typically drug addiction) by their behavior.
One who gives someone else the power to behave in a certain way.
examples: The computer is an essential enabler of the conversation.
The introduction of 33 bi-mode trains from 2023 will be an enabler for electrification of the Midland Main Line, claims East Midlands Railway Commercial Director Chris Wright.
In business, due to the stigma of alcoholism, enablers have their jobs and incomes at stake if their boss's secret is uncovered.

senses: An irrigation canal in Latin America.
A journalist.
examples: He′d been packed in with all the other journos, standing out only in that he was taller than most and didn′t make as much noise.
Journos and scribes are officially welcomed by the Taliban and then never given visas to enter. The Red Cross needs Talib approval for all journos before you can book a flight.

senses: Witches' Sabbath.
A Japanese form of archery.
ety: Japanese 弓道 (kyūdō きゅうどう), from Middle Chinese 弓 (kjuwng "bow") + 道 (dáu "Way").

senses: Cooperation between commercial competitors for their mutual advantage.
Conflict over how to divide up the benefits produced by cooperation, as for example in labor-management relations.
ety: Blend of cooperation + competition. Compare coopete.

senses: Small pellet-shaped egg pasta in Ashkenazic Jewish cuisine, made instead out of matzah during Passover.
A large wickerwork basket for carrying produce or turf.
Having God as main focus: with God, a god, or gods as the focal point.
The act of exculpating from alleged fault or crime.
That which exculpates; an excuse.
ety: Borrowed from Medieval Latin exculpātiō. By surface analysis, exculpate + -ion.

senses: A fire fighting hand tool consisting of ax or adz head on a wooden handle, used to dig a fireline.
ety: Named for a forester, Edward Pulaski, who designed the tool.
examples: A shovel, a polaski (fire axe) and a gieke can for putting out campfires, disinfectant for cleaning outhouses and picnic tables.
It was equipped with two water tanks, a pump and one inch rubber hose, plus the normal shovels, polaskis, first aid equipment, and radios.
